extracted.intended_audience: students and practitioners of journalism, political science, newspaper editors/publishers, and informed citizens interested in the role of the press
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts principles and standards for how newspapers should gather, present, and sustain news in a modern democracy, and how their economics and audiences shape content and independence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Press must make the invisible world visible
rubrics_metrics.description: The truth about distant or complex matters is not self-evident, and the machinery for assembling information is technical and expensive; without institutions and education to report the environment, 'the realities of public life' will be hidden from self-centered opinion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Requires specialized reporting institutions and educational processes; civil liberties alone do not produce accurate public opinion on complex matters. Anti-pattern: assuming truth will spontaneously emerge from free debate when dealing with an 'invisible environment.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Civil liberty (free speech) is necessary but insufficient
rubrics_metrics.description: While civil liberties (freedom of speech/press) are of fundamental practical value and must be protected, they do not guarantee accurate public opinion about complex or distant affairs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Defend civil liberties always, but supplement them with technical reporting capacity and institutions. Example: Milton/Mill-style arguments about truth emerging in free debate are limited when the subject matter is remote or complex.

rubrics_metrics.name: Newspapers should be 'free and truthful'
rubrics_metrics.description: The press is expected ethically to be 'free and truthful.' This standard is widely invoked as a normative ideal for journalism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize the normative demand but also the practical limitations: truth about complex public affairs often needs active reporting resources and interpretive apparatus, not merely freedom to speak.

rubrics_metrics.name: Economic model: circulation sold to advertisers shapes content
rubrics_metrics.description: Circulation is an asset only insofar as it can be sold to advertisers; advertisers buy the kind of circulation that reaches their customers (quality or mass), and this commercial relationship influences what newspapers publish.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating a paper, examine who its advertisers target and what audience composition it monetizes. Anti-pattern: treating the press as an arm purely of civic duty while ignoring the economic incentives created by advertising revenue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Newspapers are edited for the 'buying public'
rubrics_metrics.description: Because advertisers pay for access to readers, newspapers are edited and published primarily for the buying public—those with surplus purchasing power the advertiser wants to reach.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whose interests a newspaper serves by looking at its circulation demographics and editorial tone. Consequence: papers that alienate the buying public jeopardize their economic base and thus their survival and influence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Circulation composition: 'quality' versus 'mass' readership
rubrics_metrics.description: The kind of circulation an advertiser buys may be 'quality' (prosperous, discretionary buyers) or 'mass' (huge numbers); there is no sharp line, but different advertisers value different readerships.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether a paper pursues a quality niche or mass appeal; this choice shapes news selection, emphasis, and depth. Example: metropolitan 'key papers' that reach prosperous households are the backbone of general news gathering.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reader loyalty confers editorial independence
rubrics_metrics.description: A devoted, loyal body of readers is the greatest source of independence for a newspaper; 'more readers, more independence of the influence of advertisers; fewer readers and more dependence on the advertiser.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure independence by reader commitment and subscription habits. Anti-pattern: a paper betraying readers for advertisers—likely because publisher shares advertiser views or fears losing readers—indicates compromised independence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Payment opacity: readers expect news gratis; cost concealed via advertising
rubrics_metrics.description: Readers expect to get news virtually free; the real cost is concealed in the price of advertised commodities and in indirect subsidies, creating an anomalous ethical/economic arrangement for the press.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When judging a paper, consider how payments are structured and the hidden incentives that result. Transparency about funding (advertising, patronage, subscriptions) is a criterion for assessing potential bias.

rubrics_metrics.name: Key metropolitan papers and press associations centralize news gathering
rubrics_metrics.description: A relatively small number of metropolitan 'key papers' (cities over ~100,000) form press associations and provide general news that other local, rural, and special papers depend upon.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess news diversity and source concentration by tracking reliance on a few metropolitan outlets and wire services. Anti-pattern: assuming local papers are fully independent when they largely reprint association/wire copy.

rubrics_metrics.name: The press is judged by communal moral standards but functions economically
rubrics_metrics.description: Ethically a newspaper is judged like a church or school, yet economically it operates like a speculative business; this tension affects expectations and conduct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate newspapers both by civic/ethical norms (truthfulness, public service) and by realistic economic pressures (profit, credit, circulation growth), noting where these conflict.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public control by standards of living and audits
rubrics_metrics.description: Outside individual attention, social control should rely on devising standards of living and methods of audit so acts of public officials and industrial directors are 'plainly recorded' and their results 'objectively measured.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For news reporting about governance, prioritize stories that measure and report government performance against concrete criteria (health, housing, material necessities, education, freedom, pleasures, beauty). Anti-pattern: reporting only opinions or partisan declarations without objective metrics or audits.
